claims.text: The solidified alloy is nominally equiatomic, Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Rapid solidification produces an inherent dislocation network and a typical solute distribution in FeNiCrMn.
Dynamic strength–ductility behavior in solidified FeNiCrMn is primarily governed by rate-dependent dislocation drag arising from solute–dislocation interactions.
Post-casting subcritical annealing can systematically vary dislocation density and solute atmospheres.
Changing the initial dislocation density and solute atmosphere through heat treatment modulates the activation energy for dislocation glide.
High strain rates are associated with high dislocation velocities.
Higher dislocation velocities enhance solute-drag effects.
Strong solute–dislocation interactions increase the activation energy for dislocation glide.
Enhanced dislocation drag at high strain rates elevates dynamic yield strength.
Enhanced solute drag promotes a work-hardening response that sustains ductility.
Reducing dislocation density or weakening the solute atmosphere diminishes rate-dependent mechanical effects.

Samples having higher dislocation density and stronger solute atmospheres will exhibit greater dynamic yield strength and work hardening at high strain rates than samples having lower dislocation density.
The proposed mechanism applies from 300 to 600 K and from 10^-3 to 10^2 s^-1.
At cryogenic temperatures or more extreme dynamic conditions, deformation twinning or phase transformation may contribute.
Stress-relaxation and strain-rate-jump tests can be used to determine activation energies associated with dislocation glide in the treated samples.
Statistically similar dynamic yield strengths, work-hardening rates, and activation energies despite significantly different dislocation densities and solute atmospheres would falsify the hypothesis.
